newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai government seen surviving financial turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Thai government seen surviving financial turmoil.

text.p: Thailand's ruling coalition was expected to survive the turmoil in country's financial sector because its partners had closed ranks and the opposition failed to seize the chance to scuttle it, analysts said on Monday.

The government, with its strong majority in parliament, was capable of crushing any opposition attempt to capitalise on the financial turmoil, which last week forced authorities to order a sweeping shake-up of the sector, politicians added.

"Even though there was some dissatisfaction among some coalition partners at the way the issue was handled, I don't think there will be any change in the government in the near future," political analyst Sukhum Naulsakul of Ramkhamhaeng University told reporters.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's six-party coalition controls 222 of the 393 seats in parliament. The core party in the administration is Chavalit's New Aspiration Party (NAP).
In a massive restructure of the industry, the authorities ordered 10 weakened finance companies to raise capital by 8.25 billion baht ($317 million).
Banks and finance companies were also told to raise provisions for sub-standard loans.
Thai markets tumbled on the news. The stock market slid to near five-year lows and lost almost five percent of its value last week and the baht initially fell on the news before steadying.
On Monday, markets appeared to have digested the news and rebounded. The stock market ended up 1.72 percent to 703.32 points.
But analysts said the financial turmoil would continue to hang over the markets in the near to medium-term until proposed measures to salvage troubled financial institutions took root.

Chavalit last week moved quickly to control damage by calling a meeting with the leader of the Chart Pattana Party, the second largest party in his six-party coalition, as rumblings emerged that his unelected Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan did not have full government support.
Some Chart Pattana sources leaked news that Amnuay had launched a series of measures since late 1996 to restore the slow economy and troubled finance sector without consulting coalition partners.
But Amnuay himself made it clear that neither he nor Central Bank Governor Rerngchai Marakanond had any reason to quit because the measures were necessary medicine for the industry.
"It is impossible that Amnuay will be sacked because he has been a good selling point for the NAP sometimes," said Sukhum.

Market analysts have applauded the firm but necessary actions taken by Amnuay to restore confidence in Thailand, which has been hit by an exodus of foreign investors, a possible downgrade of its long-term debt ratings by Moody's Investor Services, slowing growth and low exports.

However, other analysts said the opposition, led by the Democrat Party of former prime minister Chuan Leekpai, would have failed had it tried to topple the government during the current economic turmoil.
Even the opposition predicted that Chavalit's coalition would survive despite the current difficulties.
Chart Pattana, although not thrilled by the prospect, would remain with the coalition despite the NAP's eroding credibility, said Surin Pisuwan, a Democrat Party leader.
"This living dangerously (by the coalition) will go on for the time being."
Although there were other smaller coalition partners who were unhappy with the way the NAP was running the country, they would rather stay just to remain in power, he added.

Surin said he was expecting a further shake-up of staff at the central bank, stock market and Finance Ministry, saying they had lost the public's confidence but the government has given no indication that this might happen.

Last week, the government ordered the suspension of three senior central bank officials, including a deputy governor, and another two police officers for failing to adequately follow through on the prosecution of ex-officials of the ailing Bangkok Bank of Commerce for banking violations.
